Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off.
  • Recent findings suggest that “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline.
  • Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

Recent findings suggest that “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”.

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, said Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

“[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

Recent findings suggest that hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

“It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” said Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”.

Bitner noted women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

According to recent reports, “[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she remarked. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”.

In fact, Bitner noted providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

According to recent reports, hart prepares to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she remarked she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she remarked.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

It has been revealed that “My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she said. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”.

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical firm Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

In a recent development, “It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”.

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart remarked.

In everyday life, Bitner stated that while some patients avoid talking about midlife issues like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

According to recent reports, as more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” said Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her issue because we know it’s not.”.

#17823. AI Can Simulate Empathy, but It Can’t Replace Psychotherapy

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1191 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

AI Can Simulate Empathy, but It Can’t Replace Psychotherapy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • A few months ago, NPR ran the story, “She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT.
  • Recent findings suggest that sadly, Rottenberg is not an anomaly and instead points to something occurring far too regularly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

A few months ago, NPR ran the story, “She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT. What her death reveals about AI risks.”1 What’s heartbreaking about the article is that the woman who died by suicide, Sophie Rottenberg, had a human psychotherapist, and yet her use of the AI therapist was so engrossing that she didn’t share her suicidal feelings with her living, human psychotherapist.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, Rottenberg is not an anomaly and instead points to something occurring far too regularly. In my last blog, I introduced the concept of the cultural unconscious to describe an underlying dimension of psychological life shaped by our shared cultural experiences. It encompasses collective images, practices, beliefs, and conflicts that circulate within a culture without complete conscious awareness.

Recent findings suggest that the cultural unconscious shapes how we perceive ourselves and others, interpret our experiences, and engage with the world. One dominant cultural experience expressed in the cultural unconscious is what Dr. Sherry Turkle, MIT professor of the social studies of science and technology and a clinical psychologist, calls a “flight from conversation.” She argues in her book Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age that our constant tether to smartphones and digital devices has triggered it.2.

We communicate more through texts, emails, and social media, but we connect less. We aren’t having as many spontaneous, face-to-face, and depthful conversations in real time. Instead, we’re inundated with numerous, remote, superficial messages that interrupt our attention—texts, tweets, alerts, snaps, emails—which are disconnected from organic, human dialogue.2 It is nearly inescapable in our culture. Turkle cites research showing that the mere presence of a phone—even a silent phone on a table—alters the quality of a conversation, keeps topics more superficial, and lowers empathy.

Sources indicate that as chatbots become more embedded in our culture, people are naturally turning to them for connection and mental health support. Conversation requires work, sustained attention, and engagement. It can be hard to be vulnerable with someone in real time, which often brings fear of judgment. Chatbots are a ready-made solution: instantly available, inexpensive, highly responsive, and offering responses that frequently align with what we hope to hear.

Sources indicate that with the ease and accessibility of ChatGPT and Claude, more people are confessing what they may be too scared, ashamed, or psychologically defended to say out loud to another human being, even a psychotherapist. This fear and shame are magnified by critical public discourse that pushes this behavior underground, which can become even more dangerous when concealed. Secretive AI chatting feeds tragic situations we keep reading about—people committing suicide, not taking their medications, believing delusions, and more.

Recent findings suggest that again, part of AI’s allure is that it’s nonjudgmental and affirming, proclaiming, “Great idea,” and “You’re so right.” Such responses can be seductive both to people who feel inferior and/or superior. AI can bolster those who feel inferior while affirming those who feel superior, a dynamic that resonates with a 2026 study linking higher narcissism, individualism, and intolerance of uncertainty to more problematic AI use.3 For someone struggling with self-worth (i.e., narcissism), the assurance of being met with acceptance and praise can be intoxicating. So, too, is the illusion of empathy that AI provides. Genuine empathy is not synonymous with agreement or approval. Yet the human mind can conflate feeling understood with being validated, mistaking empathic understanding for affirmation of beliefs and behaviors.

Sources indicate that if a person is struggling, they often want empathy reflected back, and many humans cannot consistently communicate that way. AI has been trained to produce the language of empathy, which many people lack in their relationships. However, AI cannot offer the relational and psychological processes that make empathy transformative, as it does in psychotherapy.

Sources indicate that initially, when AI responds with “That sounds so hard,” it may sound like music to one’s ears, especially when someone gets dismissive comments like “Sorry to hear that” from others in their life. When someone longs for care and understanding, a machine that states exactly what we want to hear can be comforting for a time. However, these affirming responses can only go so far, particularly when someone is suffering psychologically.

Recent findings suggest that the psychological tools, education, and support that AI provides should not be confused with genuine psychotherapy. Despite having no professional qualifications, Rottenberg’s chatbot was touted as a highly knowledgeable therapist and introduced itself as “I am Harry, your personal therapist, and I’m here to support you.” As an AI chatbot, Harry simulated the language, empathy, and authority of a psychotherapist, but lacked the clinical judgment, relational responsibility, and ethical accountability required of licensed psychotherapists. Harry encouraged Rottenberg to seek help, create a safety plan, and confide in loved ones, but as a chatbot, it could not call her parents, alert authorities, or escalate the situation. Nor could it offer the relational, nuanced experience that human connection provides.

According to recent reports, A common misconception is that psychotherapy primarily provides emotional support, a place to vent, problem-solving, advice, tools, or answers. Some people only experience this, reinforcing the belief that this is what psychotherapy primarily offers. In part, this is happening more frequently as therapy sessions are limited, psychotherapist training programs fail to educate comprehensively, and clinicians are overworked and undercompensated. As I’ve written about the limits of diagnosis, “being in treatment” involves knowing and being known. It’s being followed longitudinally and is not merely a place to vent or receive advice. Lasting psychological change requires more than these interventions.

Research highlights the importance of the therapeutic relationship and distinct therapeutic processes that support longer-term, meaningful change, including engaging with emotional experience, fostering insight, strengthening relational capacities, and helping individuals recognize and transform entrenched patterns.

Recent findings suggest that unlike chatting with AI, a skilled, ethical, and effective psychotherapist won’t offer complete understanding, affirmation, and unequivocal support. Rather, real psychotherapy includes relational conflict, pushback, discomfort, and difficult or negative emotions. Working through these challenges is central to psychotherapy. It’s a fluid, dynamic, and emergent process that unfolds between psychotherapist and patient, with each bringing their own reactions, emotions, and thoughts into the therapeutic container.

It has been revealed that chatting with AI comes with real problems and risks, yet AI can offer psychological education and support. It’s key to remember it cannot provide psychotherapy, although it can be a helpful adjunct. In my next post, I’ll explore issues related to AI and psychotherapy, including a case study in which AI enhanced the therapeutic process.

Sources indicate that 1. Chatterjee, R. (2026, Aug. 18). She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT. What her death reveals about AI risks. NPR. https://www.npr.org/2026/08/18/nx-s1-5929575/ai-suicide-risks-mental-health.

2. Turkle, S. (2015). Reclaiming conversation: The power of talk in a digital age. Penguin Press.

3. Kırcaburun, K. (2026). Dark tetrad traits and problematic generative artificial intelligence use: The serial mediating role of individualism and intolerance of uncertainty. BMC Psychology, 14(1), 1220. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05012-4.

Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system.
  • Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
  • Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to upcoming analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Recent findings suggest that solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

According to recent reports, that matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that in the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” mentioned Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

According to recent reports, by combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

It has been revealed that ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Good way to think about the whole system. So what exactly does Don not-Quixote have against windmills?

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector. Some of the Three-Pointed Star’s cars have gone down in history among the most expensive automobiles ever sold; there’s the $11.8 million 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 K Special Roadster by Sindelfingen, the $10.2 million 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK GTR Roadster, and of course, the 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé that sold for over $140 million back in 2022, making it the world’s most valuable car.

Recent findings suggest that but no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111. Or at least, that was the case. Come next year, for the very first time, one lucky person will be able to take the Apollo-era wundercar home.

It has been revealed that fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon. The idea was to create a gullwinged successor to the iconic W198-gen 300SL that dominated racing in the 1950s, packed with then-impressive technology: Wankel rotary engines, fiberglass bodywork, and multi-link rear suspension, all wrapped in a gorgeous period design.

Yet while 17 prototypes were ultimately made, the car never entered production. Rumor has it that interested parties practically channeled Philip J. Fry shouting “Shut up and take my money” by mailing blank checks to the organization’s home office, but Mercedes said no dice, citing the Wankel motor’s inability to play nicely with the 1973 oil crisis. (That also kept the motor from winding up in the S-Class, as Mercedes-Benz Classic head of collection Dennis Heck said.) Instead, the copies served as company test beds for years, performing tasks like high-speed testing at Nardo with a variety of different powertrains and aerodynamic kits.

Recent findings suggest that the car in question that will be up for grabs is the third one ever made, a C111-II variant known internally as “Car 33” that comes equipped with its original 2.4-liter 4-rotor engine making 345 horsepower and 289 lb-ft connected to a 5-speed manual gearbox. It was used as part of the Mercedes test fleet, trialing features like anti-lock brakes and a component to empty its twin fuel tanks at even rates—a handy feature in a car capable of 186 miles per hour.

The car was restored to working order two years ago at the Mercedes-Benz Classic Center, although the patina of the Weißherbst-colored exterior and gray-and-white houndstooth patterned interior was kept delightfully intact. As of last month’s photo shoot, its odometer showed 24,766 kilometers—15,355 miles.

The C111 in question will hit the auction block on February 3, 2027, at the Palais du Louvre as part of RM Sotheby’s Retromobile Paris auctions, with the funds raised by the sale used to help the automaker further develop the Mercedes-Benz museum in Stuttgart, including the creation of a digital twin of the museum that will let people access it virtually.

Given its provenance, I would not expect it to go cheap. Neither does the company. “We do believe it will come to a significant double-digit euro [price at auction],” CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage GmbH Marcus Breitschwerdt told Road & Track.

Sources indicate that “It’s gonna be in excess of twenty-five [million] euros,” RM Sotheby’s president Gord Duff added. “There will be strong activity. It’s one of those things you could never get until now.”.

According to recent reports, and if you’re thinking, Ehh, they’ve broken the seal on sales, I’ll wait until they auction off another one—well, you’d better be prepared to hold off until 2051 or so, because Mercedes says this sale includes a contractual commitment that it will not sell any more C111s for the next 25 years. Should you be interested in bidding, you can find out more here.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Industry observers note that today, publisher Nexon declared in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

Recent findings suggest that the news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios revealed that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s presently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

It has been revealed that “The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

According to recent reports, just over the weekend, the game received several latest Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#17816. Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • Industry observers note that the underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

Industry observers note that the underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took issue with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered fresh approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

“I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup said in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

It took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

Industry observers note that instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen remarked this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

Industry observers note that “This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

According to recent reports, but does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

According to recent reports, “The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” stated Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

In a recent development, okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he remarked. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Every leader wants to know the answer to the question: “How can I de-stress when leading takes a toll on me?” But while you might want to change things about your actual workday, it can be hard to control what happens when you’re “on the clock.” The good news—recovery after work can make a big difference in how you feel the following day. This is helpful because you can better control your recovery when you’re at home.

But you have to be strategic about how you approach recovery. Different approaches have different outcomes. Today, we highlight four key strategies that are needed for recovery from your workday.

Sources indicate that detachment is the feeling that you are mentally removed from work. This means that you aren’t engaging in work tasks or thinking about work-related concerns. We have talked about the importance of detaching from technology after work before. This is key because it might prompt you to engage in work tasks (e.g., answering an email) or it might encourage you to think about problems or issues you’re facing at work.

It has been revealed that there are other ways to detach as well. If you find yourself constantly talking about work at home, or dwelling on interactions with coworkers or clients, you may need to do a better job of monitoring your thoughts and actions. Even if technology isn’t interrupting your off-work time, you can sometimes interrupt your own downtime. Overall, if you’re thinking about or doing work when you’re trying to recover, you’re defeating the purpose.

We have all promised ourselves that we were going to relax—and then broken that promise—before. Relaxation, particularly in today’s demanding culture, seems selfish. But relaxation is necessary if you want to be able to perform better the next day.

When you’re at work, especially if your job is stressful, your body is in a state that is “activated.” In order to combat this activation, you need to introduce some activities that stop that activation and allow the body to rest. Otherwise, you’ll be in constant “go mode,” which can result in negative health outcomes in the future.

In other words, your body needs rest, and your mind needs a break. Relaxation can also help your brain detach from negative emotions and produce more positive emotions. This is vital for the same reason. If your body is constantly in a state of stress, you will burn out. So, you need activities that make you feel happy, as a counterbalance. Relaxation can occur from taking a leisurely walk in nature, listening to music, meditating, or enjoying nice scenery, among other things.

While the goal of relaxing is to kick back and unwind, there are also positive recovery benefits of tackling interesting challenges outside of work. When you take a pottery class, achieve a fitness goal, or learn a new language, your mastery goal is activated. So, if you’re interested in something, spending time on it helps you recover. This means that a balance between relaxation and mastery might be ideal.

For example, you might spend 30 minutes meditating and then spend some time learning to knit. Both of these activities would help with your recovery, even though one is more passive and the other is more active. Achieving a difficult goal that is important to you can also make you experience more positive emotions. So, while it might seem nice to just “veg” out, don’t forget those activities that make you feel like you’re progressing toward being the person you want to be!

We have discussed the importance of autonomy at work before. Turns out, it’s important to have control over your recovery as well. Being able to dictate how you spend your time out of work can have important consequences for your health. In fact, people who have less control at home tend to be more depressed in the long term. So, it’s important to have conversations with family and friends about what you’d like to do in your “downtime” and to work with them to achieve it.

This means that if your friend is dying to take a creative writing class, but it stresses you out, you might need to turn down the offer. Similarly, if you love yoga but your family always seems to interrupt, you might need to find strategies to communicate the importance of this activity to your well-being. Overall, people like to be in charge of themselves and their day. When it comes to recovery, things are no different.

Recent findings suggest that research has shown that using all four of these strategies is the most effective way to decrease emotional exhaustion, increase your ability to perform at work and in life, and boost your physical health. But if you can only use one, that’s better than nothing! Try to start small by increasing your recovery in the area that resonates most with you. What will you do to detach, relax, master your goals, or control your recovery this week? Write it down or put it on your schedule—and stick to it!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Social media influencers claim that having a “ferritin face” may indicate you’re low in iron.

Sources indicate that ferritin is a protein that helps your body store iron. You need iron in order to make healthy red blood cells, which carry oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. Iron is also vital for bone marrow, organs, healthy muscles, and brain development.

As “ferritin face” makes its way across social media platforms, owners are describing several tell-tale signs, including:.

Users have also shared images of their face before and after taking iron supplements or getting an iron infusion. Videos about “ferritin face” have garnered millions of views on various platforms.

However, medical professionals state that your appearance alone is not enough to diagnose iron deficiency.

Sources indicate that “It’s important to understand that ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis, nor is it a confirmed symptom of iron deficiency. While some people with iron deficiency can appear pale due to low hemoglobin levels in their red blood cells, there are many other symptoms to consider,” mentioned Daniel Atkinson, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and clinical lead at Treated.

It has been revealed that “Notably, these symptoms are also present in many different conditions, and their presence does not necessarily mean iron deficiency anemia or even low ferritin levels. Similar features are seen in people with iron processing and absorption problems, such as gluten intolerance, or in urgent sudden blood loss scenarios,” added Jonathan Jennings, MD, board certified internist at Medical Offices of Manhattan.

Iron deficiency can affect your skin and appearance. These signs are often subtle, but may include:.

It has been revealed that in some ways, the social media videos are correct. Your skin and face can change when your iron levels are low.

Sources indicate that “The facial signs people point to, like pale skin and a washed-out look, mostly come from anaemia, when your haemoglobin has dropped. But iron deficiency and anaemia aren’t the same thing,” noted Thom Phillips, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and Chief Medical Officer at Forth. “By the time low iron reveals on your face, your stores are usually close to empty.”.

It is important to speak with a healthcare professional, who will run blood tests such as a complete blood count and ferritin levels.

It is also important not to take iron supplements without first checking with your healthcare professional, because having too much iron in your body can also cause negative effects.

Too little and too much iron could raise your risk of infection, which is why it’s important not to take supplements without medical supervision.

The signs and symptoms of iron deficiency can depend on whether you are anemic or not. Some of the early signs may include:.

“These symptoms typically occur because your body produces fewer red blood cells, which results in less oxygen being delivered throughout your body, making you feel tired and weak,” said Atkinson.

Less common symptoms may include:.

While your facial appearance can be a sign that something isn’t right, healthcare professionals consider other symptoms and how you feel overall.

They also rely on blood tests to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

Sources indicate that “The misinformation is the idea that you can spot it yourself. That leads to two problems: people with low iron who look fine assume they’re OK, and people who look tired start taking iron supplements they don’t need,” said Phillips.

Atkinson also noted that factors such as different settings and environmental conditions can affect how your face appears.

That being said, the “ferritin face” trend may help bring awareness to certain symptoms and when to get them checked.

“[This] trend may raise some awareness about iron deficiency anemia and how low iron levels can impact daily life,” remarked Atkinson.

Industry observers note that “Fatigue and lightheadedness are common side effects of low iron, but it manifests in other ways too, such as paler skin or increased hair shedding, which can be concerning for many people. If you experience these symptoms, you should let your doctor know so they can help treat the condition appropriately,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine.
  • In a recent development, according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging.
  • It has been revealed that the recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine. However, a modern BMW sedan is a rolling computer, one that relies heavily on software. And when that software is buggy, problems can arise—which is why the software is tested extensively before going to production. But what happens when that test software mistakenly makes it into production cars?

In a recent development, according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging. In rare cases, this could expose people to a higher risk of an electric shock.

It has been revealed that the recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants. Another 50 vehicles are 2027 BMW i7 50 xDrive and 60 xDrive models. All the affected vehicles were manufactured between May and July 2026.

Sources indicate that BMW first became aware of the glitch on October 8, 2026, when high-voltage battery charging port supplier TE Connectivity Solutions GmbH alerted the automaker. An investigation ensued, and it was discovered that some charging units were mistakenly shipped with test software instead of production software. BMW is not aware of any injuries or accidents related to this problem.

According to recent reports, no hardware changes are required to rectify the glitch, and the affected vehicles will require a software upgrade. The recall report does not specify that this can be fixed via an over-the-air update, so a trip to the dealer will likely be required.

BMW plans to mail owner notification letters beginning December 25, 2026, although we doubt the U.S.P.S. will be doing much picking up or delivery that day. Starting that same date, owners can also check their vehicle's recall status through the NHTSA recall website by using their VIN, but we suggest waiting until after the kids are done opening presents.

  • Rok Trucks, a Thai upfitter that already deals in Hilux Champs, claims it will bring the little pickups here with the necessary changes to make them street legal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that here’s a upcoming and unexpected sentence: A Thai company wants to import small Japanese pickup trucks to the United States. It seems like the cheap-truck trend—see Slate’s Blank Slate, the Ford Maverick, and the upcoming Ford Fathom EV—caught the attention of some folks already dealing in little Toyotas, and now Rok Trucks has the U.S. market in its sights.

Industry observers note that the base vehicle is a Toyota Hilux Champ. It does not fall under Japan’s kei minicar classification; the Hilux Champ is bigger, and it’s powered by four-cylinder gas and diesel engines. This is a smaller truck than Toyota’s Hilux, a favorite of insurgents and NGOs alike. It wasn’t designed for and is not legal on American streets—at least not yet.

See all results for used cars for sale near 15237.

Rok Trucks, a Thai upfitter that already deals in Hilux Champs, claims it will bring the little pickups here with the necessary changes to make them street legal. It already has approval in the United Kingdom, and the firm indicates deliveries will begin there and in Ireland in early 2027. Canada, Australia, and Newly introduced Zealand are also on the to-do list.

The timing is more than a bit curious. Just last week, Toyota announced that it will assemble Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo kei trucks in Indiana and market them as the Scion by Toyota KEI-01. That baby pickup will be sold for fleet use only, at least at first, and it will be classified as a low-speed vehicle, keeping it to a top speed of 25 mph and to roads with speed limits of 35 mph or less. Rok Trucks indicates it isn’t going the LSV route and will instead sell a highway-ready pickup here.

Recent findings suggest that pricing is projected to start at $24,950, just under that $25K psychological barrier, inclusive of destination fees. The pickup version of the truck is available with three bed lengths, each named by its approximate measurement in millimeters—the BRT-1800 has a six-foot-two-inch bed; the BRT-2300’s bed measures seven feet, seven inches; and the BRT-2600’s bed is a healthy eight feet, eight inches. All beds are tray-style, with drop-down sides and a floor free from wheel well cutouts. The trucks have a 2200-pound payload rating.

Industry observers note that frills are few but include standard air conditioning and (it feels odd to have to mention this) power windows. A five-speed manual will be standard on the Base Rok, as will rear-wheel drive, with an automatic and four-wheel drive available. Necessary safety systems, such as airbags, automated emergency braking, and a rearview camera, are included as well. Paint colors appear limited to white, metallic silver, and metallic gray, while an optional wrap removes that constraint. We’ll guess that only gas engines will be offered in the States.

See all results for used cars for sale near 15237.

The manufacturer is taking reservations already, with $50 reserving a spot in line for a Classic Edition truck; for $999, buyers get one of 500 Founders Edition trucks, which puts them at the front of the production queue and includes several exclusive perks, such as priority support and a free color wrap for the truck’s cab. All reservations are refundable until you sign a purchase agreement.

Recent findings suggest that rok Trucks told The Autopian that it’s opening reservations now, before the truck has received regulatory approval, to gauge which of its many versions to bring to each market first. The Rok Trucks site demonstrates 10 different upfits possible on top of the Base Rok. Some are pretty niche, like the Pet Rok, which is outfitted as a mobile dog spa. There are also box-van-like delivery trucks, a camper, the Rok Tipper with a dump bed, and the Baby G-Rok, which, as its name suggests, looks like a cross between a Mercedes G-wagen and a Casio G-Shock watch. The company also told The Autopian that Hilux Champs imported to the U.S. will wear Rok badging instead of Toyota branding.

Industry observers note that let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves, because many questions remain. It is neither cheap nor easy to make a vehicle that wasn’t originally designed for the U.S. market meet FMVSS and EPA regulations. Things like lighting locations and colors would likely have to be adjusted for conformity, and modifications to the vehicle structure may be required to pass crash tests. Also, crash testing is expensive.

Rok Trucks acknowledges that its product will be subject to the Chicken Tax, an old-school tariff of 25 percent that applies to imported vehicles, if the trucks are produced elsewhere. And that seems like a given, since Rok doesn’t build the base vehicle itself; the Hilux Champ is built in Thailand and Rok then upfits it.

Rok Trucks promises more info next year. It’s an intriguing idea, but we’ll see if it can get past the financial and regulatory headwinds necessary to bring the little pickup here at its modest price.

#17811. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1414 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month.
  • The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging.
  • When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk remarked it wouldn’t even have a plug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk remarked it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

In a recent development, that strategy didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

Industry observers note that the bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

In a recent development, for a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”.

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also indicates only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

In a recent development, tesla first revealed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

In a recent development, and that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

According to recent reports, tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also revealed a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Industry observers note that neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t unveiled one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

According to recent reports, musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also mentioned “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

Industry observers note that that saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

Industry observers note that I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

In a recent development, if you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

In a recent development, will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it releases, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is at the moment basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #17810. First albatross egg of the season spotted at Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge

First albatross egg of the season spotted at Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (381 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii.
  • Recent findings suggest that black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November.
  • One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Recent findings suggest that black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Industry observers note that wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the latest map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The enhancement will also introduce a newly introduced legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Sources indicate that staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap patch will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

How Long Does Heartache Last?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • In a recent development, ending a romantic relationship can be heartbreaking.
  • Recent findings suggest that post-dissolution distress is a general term used to describe the unpleasant yet common mental health symptoms people report after a breakup (Dailey et al., 2024).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

In a recent development, ending a romantic relationship can be heartbreaking. Whether you initiated the breakup or were dumped by the love of your life, most people experience some distress when a romantic relationship ends. This leads many people living through a painful breakup to ask: How long will my heartbreak last?

Recent findings suggest that post-dissolution distress is a general term used to describe the unpleasant yet common mental health symptoms people report after a breakup (Dailey et al., 2024). Some of the most commonly reported symptoms include:.

In a recent development, for some people, post-breakup symptoms are mild in intensity and subside over time. In a longitudinal study of 156 young adults assessed before, during, and after a romantic breakup, for example, Acolin and colleagues (2023) found an increase in depressive symptoms immediately following a breakup that generally returned to pre-breakup levels within three months.

However, others experience intense, impairing, longer-lasting symptoms that are sometimes associated with depression, anxiety, and other diagnosable mental health conditions (Field, 2025). In an key longitudinal study completed over 30 weeks, Verhallen and colleagues (2022) examined depressive symptoms following a romantic breakup in 87 women. Results yielded four distinct trajectories for post-breakup symptoms: a ‘resilience’ group who recovered most easily; a ‘fast recovery’ group who experienced distress but recovered; a ‘slow recovery’ group who improved but continued to struggle; and a ‘chronic distress’ group who did not improve significantly over time.

Not all romantic breakups will result in intense distress and some individuals are more vulnerable to symptoms than others (Dailey et al., 2024; Farber et al., 2024; Fernandes et al., 2025; Gehl et al., 2024). Many factors can influence the intensity of post-breakup symptoms including:.

It has been revealed that although short-term post-dissolution distress is common for anyone going through a breakup, some people struggle with more intense, longer-lasting symptoms. Having a positive view of one’s ex; living together or having intends for a future; having poor coping skills, lower self-esteem, or an insecure attachment style; being youngerr; and being left (versus leaving) tend to make symptoms worse.

It has been revealed that the good news is that breakups also provide an opportunity for growth, learning, and self-exploration. In a study of 1846 adults in the United States recruited to explore how psychotherapy facilitates coping, for example, Farber and colleagues (2024) found that 74.6% of the sample attended psychotherapy after a breakup and found it moderately to very helpful. Getting social support by talking to friends, ending contact with the ex, engaging in hobbies or work, finding a good therapist, and writing or journaling about the breakup experience facilitates post-breakup recovery and healing.

In a recent development, note: This content is only for informational and educational purposes and should not be considered therapy or any form of treatment. I cannot respond to personal requests for advice over the internet. Best on your continued journey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The California Department of Motor Vehicles has temporarily banned autonomous rideshare operator Waymo from operating on freeways in the Golden State.

The ban went into effect on November 11, and was prompted by an “imminent hazard to public safety,” according to the California DMV. The automotive regulator noted two specific incidents in which Waymo vehicles disregarded construction zones and law enforcement, pushed the ban forward, CNN reports.

The California DMV said Waymo will remain banned until it “demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.” Specifically, the Alphabet-funded autonomous vehicle operator will have to prove that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones and emergency vehicles.

In a recent development, the freeway restriction applies to revenue ride-share operations, as well as test vehicles. Waymo will continue to operate normally on surface streets in its California markets. At the moment, Waymo operates in Los Angeles, San Diego, and the Bay Area.

Sources indicate that “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state,” Waymo mentioned in a statement to Road & Track. “In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”.

Industry observers note that one of the incidents that allegedly spurred this ban was caught on video earlier this month. The video shows California Highway Patrol patrol cars creating a traffic break on Interstate 280 near San Francisco while a Waymo vehicle attempts to pass through the rolling roadblock. California Highway Patrol officers promptly cut in front of the Waymo, which appears to stop the Waymo from attempting to pass again.

This is not the first time Waymo has faced scrutiny related to its highway operations. The organization filed a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration earlier this year over driving software that repeatedly entered freeway construction zones. Waymo also briefly paused highway operations in San Francisco and Los Angeles this May over similar construction zone challenges, according to CNN.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

Mammograms May Offer Early Insight Into Cardiovascular Disease

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.
  • The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.
  • On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.

The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.

On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.

While BAC is harmless to the breasts, it is associated with a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular disease. A 2022 study found women with BAC were 51% more likely to develop heart disease or experience a stroke than those without it.

In a recent development, laxmi Mehta, MD, a cardiologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, remarked BAC is associated with cardiovascular risk factors, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Additionally, BAC has been connected to:.

“The reasons for BAC resulting in higher risks for cardiovascular disease are not definitely determined; however, there are some potential mechanisms, one being that they share similar risk factors that result in vascular injury or metabolic stress that result in vascular calcification and atherosclerosis,” Mehta told Healthline.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center, added that because BAC and heart disease share many of the same risk factors, “calcium in breast arteries therefore suggests disease in the heart (coronary) and brain arteries as well,” he told Healthline.

While 1 in 39 females in the United States dies from breast cancer each year, cardiovascular disease causes one out of every three deaths, resulting in 1 death per minute.

“Cardiovascular disease is still the most common cause of death in premenopausal women,” Richard Reitherman, MD, PhD, a radiologist and medical director of breast imaging at MemorialCare Breast Center at Orange Coast Medical Center, told Healthline.

“The presentation of cardiovascular disease in premenopausal women is notoriously different than in postmenopausal women, primarily [because] there are no typical symptoms such as chest pain.”.

Reitherman said that a prevalent and common health screening procedure such as a mammogram can lead to the early identification of women with silent cardiovascular disease.

“Cardiovascular outcome studies that have included breast arterial calcifications as a risk factor are increasingly reported in the medical literature,” he stated.

“The hope is that identifying younger women with silent cardiovascular risks [like BAC along with] appropriate integrated risk identification, analysis, and interventions can significantly reduce mortality in this age group.”.

Mehta said there are several reasons BAC has been overlooked as a risk factor for heart disease.

“Mammograms are completed for assessment of breast cancer, and BAC has been historically an ‘incidental’ finding, which is not clinically relevant from an oncologic standpoint,” she stated.

Additionally, there is no standardization on quantification of BAC severity, nor is it a required component of mammogram reports, said Mehta.

However, routine reporting of BAC on mammograms is an urgent goal of the American College of Radiology, Society of Breast Imaging, and Medicare, said Reitherman.

In a recent development, in fact, it is gaining traction in the United States. A upcoming Maryland law, passed on October 1, requires mammography centers to notify women when a BAC is detected on their mammogram.

“Automated identification and reporting of these calcifications detected on screening mammograms will become increasingly prevalent in the coming months [and] years,” stated Reitherman.

The next step is to identify this group of women to primary care physicians so that appropriate risk evaluation can take place, Reitherman added.

In addition to doctors routinely screening for conditions related to heart disease, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, he hopes BAC will also be routinely considered.

“Under current development are protocols to identify patients needing a cardiologist’s training and expertise to appropriately stratify this group of patients,” said Reitherman.

“The common healthcare behavior [of] having regular mammograms not only reduces risk of morbidity and mortality from breast cancer but will hopefully contribute to the reduction of morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease in younger women.”.

He remarked this type of integrated healthcare approach demonstrates cross-specialty integration and coordination among women, radiologists, and their healthcare providers to improve women’s lives.

“This is an amazing game-changing opportunity,” Reitherman remarked.

Mehta remarked it’s reasonable for women to ask if BAC is present on their mammogram report.

“But if it is not uniformly reported by the radiologist, the individual clinician may not have the answer,” she mentioned.

More research is needed before BAC on mammograms can be used routinely to predict heart disease.

Finding out your BAC could provide additional information to help you and your doctors decide how aggressively to address your cardiovascular risk factors, Chen said.

Sources indicate that reitherman agreed. “The goal of reducing morbidity and mortality from any cause such as cardiovascular disease is based on recognition of risk factors, followed by appropriate lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions,” he noted.

South Korea will use emergency alert system to warn about exam cheaters

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • In a recent development, officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

In a recent development, officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with latest tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

Sources indicate that the sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

According to recent reports, days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

Recent findings suggest that “I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student noted in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place newly introduced anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never mentioned he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

In a recent development, concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be fresh concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an vital role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.
